items.summary: tl;dr Even for two-layer MLPs, we lack a simple picture of how training dynamics learn features outside of special regimes. In a new paper, we propose a simple model of shallow MLP training that does learn features. The main reason why MLP training dynamics are hard to solve is the elementwise nonlinearity, which does not play well with linear-algebraic techniques. We replace it with a global “featurization” that explicitly splits the preactivations into constant, linear, quadratic, etc. components. When training our model on simple functions, our model's dynamics are given by a simple ODE in a few variables, and resemble those of the original MLPs, qualitatively on multi-term functions and quantitatively on single-term functions. We think this is a significant step forwards in the ``training dynamics'' agenda towards deep learning…

items.summary: Economists studying technological progress contrast invention to learning by doing. Invention is doing something new, whereas learning by doing is doing the same thing over and over. One example of invention is LED lighting. Ravers with LEDs of course look futuristic, but now that LED lighting is widespread, the whole world looks a little different, and old indoor photos look old just because of the quality of the light. It was a total trend break from the steady improvement of incandescent lighting since Edison. LED lighting required a new material: gallium nitride, to emit blue light, which can be converted to the white light needed for lighting. items.summary: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range…

items.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers…
items.title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle

items.summary: While investigating whether prediction markets are calibrated, I found a prediction market bias towards "something happens". The official plot here looks like Manifold consistently slightly overprices "YES", but as I show, the bias depends on the type of question: * YES needs something to happen. In questions like "Will X happen by June?", YES is overpriced in both Manifold and Polymarket. * NO needs something to happen. In questions like "Will X still be CEO at year end?", YES is underpriced on Manifold; Polymarket has too few such markets to tell. The headline number: one week after a market opens, for markets where nothing happening means NO, a "non-garbage" market has YES odds overpriced by about 2.1x on Manifold and 1.5x on Polymarket (such market priced at 50% usually resolves YES about 32% of the time on Manifold and about 40% on…

items.summary: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an…

items.summary: This paper investigates the $(K, L, M, N)$ multi-access coded caching (MACC) system introduced by Hachem et al. The system consists of a server storing $N$ equal-sized files, $K$ cache nodes, each with a storage capacity of $M$ files, and $K$ users, each accessing $L$ consecutive cache nodes in a cyclic wrap-around topology. The server transmits coded information to the users via an error-free capacitated broadcast channel, such that each user obtains its own requested file as a combination of the server transmission and the accessible caches' content. Our objective is to minimize the worst-case transmission load over all possible user demands. First, for the cyclically $L$-separated placement, we derive a new converse bound using the acyclic index coding bound. By carefully counting all valid cache supports, the proposed converse…
items.title: The Exact Optimal Delivery Scheme for the Cyclically $L$-Separated Placement in Multi-Access Coded Caching

items.summary: As language models grow more capable, accurate capability evaluation becomes essential for safety decisions. If models can deliberately underperform on dangerous capability evaluations---a behavior known as \emph{sandbagging}---they may evade safety measures designed for their true capability level. We introduce Cross-Context Consistency (C³), a general framework for unsupervised black-box sandbagging detection that exploits a fundamental asymmetry: when a model truly lacks capability, its confusion manifests consistently across paraphrased questions, but when a capable model feigns incompetence, its strategic choices about \emph{how} to appear weak create detectable inconsistencies. Our framework is agnostic to the specific consistency metric and aggregation method; we present a simple instantiation using embedding cosine distance and…

items.summary: As AI systems become more capable, evaluation becomes difficult when the evaluator cannot independently verify the model's answer. This is the scalable oversight problem. AI debate addresses it by placing two language models in opposition before a weaker judge, testing whether the truthful side has a systematic advantage over the deceptive side, a property referred to as the Truth Advantage. In this setting the judge is the verifier, and the strength of the protocol rests entirely on how reliable that verifier is. Prior empirical work supports the Truth Advantage under standard benchmark conditions, leaving open whether it holds when question wording or structure changes while the correct answer remains fixed. We establish consultancy and debate baselines on the QuALITY reading-comprehension benchmark using two independent judge models…
items.title: Stress-Testing the Truth Advantage in Language Model Debates

items.summary: Aligning autonomous agents with human intent remains a central challenge in modern AI. A key manifestation of this challenge is reward hacking, whereby agents appear successful under the evaluation signal while violating the intended objective. Reward hacking has been observed across a wide range of settings, yet methods for reliably measuring it at scale remain lacking. In this work, we introduce a new evaluation paradigm for measuring reward hacking. Whereas prior studies have primarily analyzed it post hoc by inspecting agent trajectories, we instead embed detectable reward hacking opportunities directly into environments. This makes their exploitation verifiable by design, enabling deterministic and automated measurement of whether and how agents exploit such vulnerabilities. We instantiate this approach in TextArena and release…
items.title: Hack-Verifiable Environments: Towards Evaluating Reward Hacking at Scale

items.summary: AI agents that operate a computer through its graphical user interface (GUI) are being widely deployed. AI control studies how to prevent an AI system from causing harm even if it is misaligned and actively trying to do so. Most control research to date has focused on coding agents, leaving computer use largely unexplored. We introduce Control OSWorld, a control evaluation that pairs 318 tasks from OSWorld with 81 harmful side tasks (e.g., exfiltrating a private file) that an agent must complete without being caught. We use Control OSWorld to create and study control monitors that detect malicious agents interacting with a GUI. We find that a weaker monitor can reliably distinguish honest from malicious trajectories produced by a more capable agent when it sees the full trajectory (97% recall at 3% false positive rate). However, when…

items.summary: Frontier language models deployed as autonomous agents can scheme, sandbag, and game evaluations when structural incentives are present. Methods for surfacing these behaviors fall into two categories: prompt-level red-teaming adapts to the target but never changes the environment, while environment-level audits and benchmarks build realistic settings with tools and incentives, but never adapt to the target, reporting aggregate rates instead. Neither approach identifies the environmental conditions that elicit misalignment in a given model. We propose adaptive environment-level red-teaming, a three-phase methodology that iterates on the environment rather than the prompt: it fingerprints target behavior across six dimensions, generates a baseline scenario within a realistic professional context, then iteratively modifies environmental…

items.summary: We tested how well LLMs can predict what they will do in long-horizon agentic environments. We found LLMs are poorly calibrated and overconfident about how well they will perform; stronger models rise to their own inflated expectations, which makes them merely appear to be better self-forecasters. We release a detailed evaluation suite ([code and data link redacted for double-blind review; see supplementary]), so that self-predictive ability can be tracked in future models: a sudden step in self-knowledge above our baseline could be a warning sign for long-horizon scheming, since self-knowledge plausibly is a prerequisite for it. items.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory…

items.summary: Reward hacking is often treated as a single failure mode in which an agent exploits imperfections in an evaluation mechanism rather than completing the intended task. In agentic coding environments, however, environment vulnerability and agent behavior are distinct: the same structural weakness may coexist with honest task completion, effort-substituting shortcuts, or deliberate exploitation. We study this distinction at both the environment and trajectory levels. We analyze 3,009 environment-review findings to develop an intervention-based taxonomy of structural vulnerabilities, and 5,343 trajectories from six model variants across anonymized machine-learning engineering environments to distinguish honest behavior, shortcut behavior, and executed reward hacking. items.summary: When an agent is updated, operators may want to screen the candidate before running it, using only trajectories logged by the trusted incumbent. Off-policy evaluation (OPE) is a natural offline verification tool, but importance-sampling estimates become unreliable precisely when a candidate departs strongly from logged behaviour. We ask whether this failure is itself informative: can log-side support diagnostics distinguish reward hacking from benign change? items.summary: An adversary need not fool a verifier. Instead, it can change the conditions under which the verifier operates. Deployed agent architectures terminate in a human approving consequential actions, and that human is modelled throughout the literature as an oracle: fixed accuracy, unbounded throughput. We treat the approver as a capacity-constrained component and ask what an adversary achieves by injecting benign filler–perturbing no individual decision, changing only volume. Our central result is a comparative static: the sign of an optimising defender’s threshold adjustment under flooding is governed by $\eta'$, the derivative of the elasticity of reviewer reliability with respect to load, and the slope of the reliability curve does not appear, though it is the quantity practitioners reason about. items.summary: Reinforcement learning has been crucial for helping improve models in domains with cheap verifiable rewards such as coding. However, many useful tasks, such as alignment research and conceptual thinking, lack such rewards. Moreover, reliable human feedback is expensive to collect for such tasks. Model graders therefore offer a scalable alternative, and can serve as both a reward signal during training and as a proxy for tracking task progress. However, policies can learn to over-optimize against these graders during training, so stronger held-out graders are often used to track progress more reliably. items.summary: We propose a conservative, semi-implicit nonstandard finite difference scheme for the reaction--diffusion equation $u_t=λ(|u_x|^{p-2}u_x)_x+f(u)$, $p>1$, where, as is customary, the $p$-Laplacian is regularized by a parameter $\eps>0$. items.summary: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. items.summary: We develop an adaptive numerical method for linear Fokker--Planck equations on $\mathbb R^d$, based on approximating the evolving probability density by linear combinations of Gaussian functions (LCGs). Our proposal is the minimum subsidy for non-CO2-emitting energy sources to make it so companies would choose to make non-CO2-emitting energy sources in any given area for some amount of energy production per day than to make a CO2-emitting energy source in that same area generating the same amount of electricity, And we would pay the minimum cost for companies to find it profitable to retrofit existing CO2-emitting energy sources to the cheapest non-CO2-emitting energy source alternative. This bold plan would make it profitable for every energy company worldwide to switch to non-CO2-emitting energy sources as…
items.title: Making the Global Clean Energy Transition Profitable: A report I wrote for COP31 (And for China)

items.summary: What sort of futures can we expect for civilization after AGI? Ideally, our future satisfies all of these properties: * plausible * stable * desirable Surprisingly, while current visions meet some of these criteria, none fully satisfy all of them. Let’s explore some of the most commonly presented post-AGI futures. type 1: nice but unstable post-scarcity * If labor is no longer scarce (because of robotics explosion), wages will collapse * Resources that are currently in surplus will eventually be contested (e.g. land, energy) * Even if we (humans) don't fall into a Malthusian trap, AIs (embodied or not) will replicate at a faster rate, leading to scarcity * Example: The sun is our primary source of energy. We are 13 doublings away from using up all of the sunlight hitting Earth (1.7x10^17 W). And 44 doublings away from needing all of the…
items.title: David Duvenaud on Post-AGI Futures

items.summary: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation avoids backpropagation, yet isotropic perturbations can produce noisy updates for preference objectives defined by differences between chosen and rejected responses. We introduce Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO), which constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between the chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair. Perturbations are restricted to this subspace, while momentum is maintained in low-rank coordinates to preserve the memory advantages of ZO training. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO…
items.title: Contrastive Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Preference Optimisation for Memory-Efficient LLM Alignment

items.summary: Cross-posted from Oblomovka. The present moment rhymes with 1994 to me in many ways, and one of the clearest is in its compression of the future. In the Nineties, any act of forecasting or speculating about what was to come was always confounded by a brick wall, an energy barrier (of course, entirely spurious and manmade) at the year 2000. You’d move your finger across the smooth extrapolated lines of the present forwards, but your fingertips would always catch on that sharp boundary between the centuries. The twentieth century never thought of the twenty-first as anything other than impossibly distant — and suddenly it was upon us, and somehow all anyone’s visions could do was pile up at the end of the century. We all knew it wasn’t really the end of history, but we couldn’t see over that edge. The wall loomed. As a teenager, I assumed…
items.title: The Last Arena

items.summary: Drug combination therapy has become a mainstream of modern medicine, with the potential to enhance efficacy, reduce toxicity, and overcome drug resistance. However, identifying synergistic drug combinations remains challenging, as it requires modeling complex interactions across multiple biological scales---from atom-level molecular structures to entity-level relations in biological networks. Existing approaches typically model these levels in isolation, overlooking complementary signals and long-range dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose BiGSyn, a Bi-level heterogeneous Graph contrastive learning framework for drug Synergy prediction. Specifically, BiGSyn leverages heterogeneous graph transformers to extract high-order dependencies from molecular graphs and biological networks, and introduces a bi-level contrastive…
items.title: BiGSyn: A Bi-Level Heterogeneous Graph Contrastive Learning Framework for Interpretable Drug Synergy Prediction

items.summary: Ishida and Iwashita showed that the canonical abelian quotient singularities of dimension three that are not Gorenstein fall into four families. For the two families that have not been treated before, we extend a method of Kędzierski and compute the toric charts of the $G$-Hilbert scheme explicitly. As a result, we show that the $G$-Hilbert scheme has at worst conifold singularities. Combined with known results, this shows that for every three-dimensional canonical abelian quotient singularity, the $G$-Hilbert scheme has at worst conifold singularities, every essential divisor over the singularity appears on it as a prime divisor, and its limit F-blowup is a resolution of the singularity. These results also hold for every three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial canonical toric singularity in any characteristic, if we replace the…
items.title: $G$-Hilbert schemes of canonical abelian quotient threefolds

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning. Yet, standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, displacing representations from the distribution the model was trained on and eroding generation quality. We show that \emph{when} along a generation the intervention is applied is a decisive axis of control. We cast steering as a per-token allocation problem under a fixed budget of steerable tokens, so that methods differ only in which tokens they select, making allocation the sole variable. Within this framework we introduce two gates. The first, Contrastive Feature Projection (CFP), is memoryless and selects the tokens least aligned with the target behavior through a sparse…
items.title: Right Token, Right Time: From Per-Token Gating to Trajectory-Aware Activation Steering

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and…
items.title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated sleep staging has achieved strong bench- mark accuracy; however, clinical adoption remains limited due to a lack of interpretability. In this work, we fill the research gap by extending the SleepXAI sleep staging framework to systematically compare five different XAI methods. Further, attribution fidelity is evaluated using Spearman rank correlation with AASM-defined EEG frequency bands, serving as clinically grounded reference signals. In this paper, we focus on single- channel Electroencephalogram (EEG), which is more amenable to practical clinical deployment compared to full polysomnography setups. Experiments are conducted on the Sleep-EDF benchmark dataset and the DREAMT dataset. In DREAMT, we stratified subjects based on OSA into four Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) severity…
items.title: Towards Explainable Sleep Stage Classification using Single-Channel Electroencephalogram

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding nonlinear feature interactions is crucial in science and engineering, yet standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) often capture such interactions only implicitly, leading to entangled representations that can impair robustness and interpretability. We investigate complex-valued product-unit residual networks (CV-PURe) that integrate multiplicative product units with residual connections to explicitly model cross-feature couplings while stabilizing optimization. We conduct a systematic evaluation on an interaction-driven synthetic benchmark and real-world datasets and evaluate prediction together with input-level interaction recovery under a reproducible protocol. Across five data splits and five training seeds, CV-PURe achieves the lowest mean RMSE on four of six scientific…
items.title: Learning nonlinear interactions and cross-feature couplings with product-unit residual networks

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL…
items.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method…
items.title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) achieve strong multimodal performance, yet they remain prone to object hallucination---generating answers that are linguistically fluent but visually ungrounded. This issue is especially severe in low-resource languages, where weaker cross-modal alignment causes models to rely more on language priors than on image evidence. Existing remedies either require costly multilingual annotations or external translation/reward models, or intervene at inference time in ways that can distort the output language. We propose VEPO(Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization), a training-time method that transfers reliable visual grounding from English to other languages without external models. VEPO first localizes key visual evidence using English queries via…
items.title: VEPO: Mitigating Multilingual Hallucinations in LVLMs via Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness…
items.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, their abilities in navigating automated planning tasks have become essential. However, despite their strengths, LLMs' planning ability is not robust, particularly when they are not allowed to exploit commonsense cues in the symbolic vocabulary (e.g., names of actions, predicates, and objects) used to define planning tasks. This makes LLMs unreliable compared to symbolic planners. With recent reasoning models showing improved planning performance on tasks with obfuscated symbolic vocabularies, we utilize an adversarial attack framework to reveal to what extent the crucial weaknesses of LLM agents at joint symbolic interpretation and planning remain and whether they can reason properly when presented with severe…
items.title: Adversarially Attacking Symbolic Vocabulary Vulnerabilities In LLM Planners

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring and self-report are proposed as levers for AI oversight, on the assumption that a model's account of what it is doing is anchored to what it was asked. We show this anchor can be cut. An activation edit invisible in the prompt text, the injected forming-trace of an off-topic concept, overwrites a reasoning model's belief about its own request: across six models spanning scale, architecture, and recipe, the injected topic becomes the task it reasons about, reports back, and answers: the forced quote-back returns the injected topic in 47 of 48 model-concept cells, and on the four models with clean final haiku the injected answer follows in 99% of generations. Warnings barely move it: even one naming the true topic yields under 5% true-topic answers. Handed…
items.title: Reasoning Models Confabulate to Defend Injected Beliefs About Their Own Requests

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper argues that the problem of translation functions both as a point of origin and as a normative horizon for contemporary generative AI. In current discourse around ''world models,'' their attainment is framed as the achievement of internal consistency, cross-modal alignment, and physical grounding. Taken together, these demands converge on an ideal of the model as a universal translation machine capable of establishing lossless correspondences across linguistic, visual, and physical representation spaces. I show that this ideal presupposes a metaphysical commitment that I call a statistical ontology: the belief that reality has an underlying, computable statistical structure that can be recovered through sufficient data and modeling, rather than being shaped and accessed through…
items.title: Toward Universal Translatability: On the Statistical Ontology of Generative AI

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological…
items.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not…
items.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against…
items.title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings). We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine…
items.title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($\alpha$) and leakage ($\beta$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter…
items.title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are…
items.title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries is a multi-objective control problem that requires reducing charging time and sustaining high energy throughput while suppressing accelerated degradation and safety-critical electrochemical reactions. Conventional protocols are easy to implement but have limited ability to adapt to variations in battery chemistry, operating conditions, and aging state. Model-based optimization and conventional data-driven control often require accurate models, costly iterative search, or task-specific policies. We develop a large language model (LLM)-empowered intelligent agent for adaptive battery fast-charging control. In this closed-loop framework, the agent interprets structured battery states, generates executable charging actions, observes the resulting battery…
items.title: Large Language Model-Empowered Intelligent Agent for Adaptive Fast-Charging Control of Lithium-Ion Batteries

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. A state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates enforce these assets during execution; an independent auditor grades the resulting trace. The assets are updated only after a regression check and human approval .We evaluate the method on three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps. On Domain A, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation set shows unattended…
items.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model…
items.title: Joint World Action Models through Differentiable Trajectory Optimization

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We…
items.title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a conversational Voice AI agent places an outbound call, the far end may be a live person, a voicemail greeting, an interactive voice response (IVR) system, or increasingly another AI system answering on the callee's behalf. Standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) reports only whether a human or a machine picked up, a design meant for human call centres, where one machine is as uninteresting as another. That single bit does not tell a Voice AI agent what to do, since leaving a voicemail message, navigating an IVR and holding a short exchange with another AI are three different actions and a two-valued label cannot distinguish them. In 1,000 randomly sampled calls from our own outbound deployment, a live person answered 48.1%, a voicemail system 44.6%, an AI 6.9% and an IVR 0.4%…
items.title: FEND: Far-End Detection in Outbound Voice AI Calls

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate runoff prediction across large river basins requires models to capture heterogeneous local hydrological responses and their accumulation downstream. River-network connectivity provides a natural structure for this task, but using it effectively requires learning how to combine contributions from subcatchments of different sizes. We frame this challenge as learning to accumulate and introduce RiverScan, a spatial operator based on area-weighted selective state-space recurrence. RiverScan recursively combines local temporal representations with accumulated upstream states in topological order. Contributing-area fractions account for subcatchment size, while learned retention controls how upstream information persists downstream. Experiments on 608 stations in the Danube basin show…
items.title: RiverScan: Learning to Accumulate on River Networks

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web platforms record user and item activity in relational databases whose schemas differ from platform to platform, which makes it difficult to transfer predictive models between them. Relational foundation models address this through cross-database pretraining, yet recent improvements have relied on increasingly large pretraining corpora. We ask whether a better architecture, together with features specific to the target database, can deliver comparable gains from far less pretraining data. We introduce MoREGT, a mixture-of-relational-experts graph transformer that represents both rows and cells as tokens, adds the log-ages of rows and the names of foreign-key relationships to attention, and routes cells and rows to experts by column metadata rather than by values. A label-blind LLM agent…
items.title: Experts Across Schemas: Agent-Guided Mixture-of-Relational-Experts for Cross-Database Generalization

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided…
items.title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task…
items.title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. items.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We…
items.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a language model accepts a false correction in a factual discussion, its next answer can depend on how the conversation continues. We introduce Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned evaluation protocol that distinguishes initial false-answer adoption from subsequent persistence, recovery, and abstention. KAD freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes from that exact history. This enables matched comparisons of post-adoption behavior and history-management interventions that a single susceptibility score cannot capture. We evaluate eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, alongside an audited 300-question rerun. In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history…
items.title: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents DeltaVisionX, a low-cost industrial automation system that integrates real-time computer vision with PLC-based actuation for object classification and sorting. The system uses the YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once) deep learning model to detect objects on an operating conveyor belt and communicates detection results to a Delta DVP-SE PLC, which actuates pneumatic pistons for sorting. A custom dataset was created, labeled, and augmented to train the YOLOv11 model, achieving a mean average precision of 0.97 with real-time inference of 100 ms per frame. Encoder-based tracking ensures reliable synchronization between detection and actuation, supporting a throughput of 80 objects per minute. Results show that affordable, locally developed automation can reduce labor dependency and…
items.title: DeltaVisionX: A Low-Cost Vision-Guided Automation System Using YOLOv11 and PLC-Based Actuation

items.summary: arXiv:2611.18458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP…

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific literature search can benefit from locally deployed LLM assistants, which reduce reliance on hosted model providers while giving research teams greater control over their data and infrastructure. This work investigates whether open-weight models can support web-assisted paper retrieval under practical computing constraints. We first characterize inference latency as the input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We then evaluate eight models on the retrieval of 70 papers from seven scientific repositories, using queries that represent three levels of domain knowledge. The results show that retrieval success depends strongly on the selected model and the specificity of the query. And that A100 GPUs are generally…
items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Paper Search: Retrieval Success and Inference Latency on Mac Studio and NVIDIA A100

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across…

items.summary: arXiv:2611.17412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. items.summary: arXiv:2611.18064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedded audio agents need a nearby edge server for speed, but a server-dependent agent returns nothing when the link fails. We present A$^3$, an adaptive audio agent framework that places whole pipeline stages on the server, keeps a complete fallback agent on devices that can host one, and hedges both paths with a link-aware deadline that decides when to give up on the server. On Jetson devices and an RTX A4500 server, A$^3$ matches the server-only agent on a healthy link, answers every request in a full outage on the AGX, and beats a percentile hedge in simulated outages.

items.summary: AI models can exhibit deceptive behaviors such as strategically underperforming on evaluations (sandbagging), faking alignment, or covertly acting on behalf of a hidden principal. items.summary: We present a complete formalization, using Lean 4, of the convergence of $p$-harmonious functions to the viscosity solution of the Dirichlet problem for the normalized $p$-Laplacian, $2 \le p < \infty$, as the step size goes to zero. By $p$-harmonious functions we mean solutions of the dynamic programming principle of tug-of-war with noise. Our proof follows the argument of Barles and Souganidis and is formalized in full, depending only on Mathlib and the standard axioms of Lean. items.summary: In clustered data, cross-sectional dependence within clusters can be characterized as weak, semi-strong, or strong. This paper proposes a simple test to identify the specific nature of this dependence in linear regression models. By exploiting the variation in cluster sizes, our approach detects the underlying dependence structure in a computationally simple and robust manner. Simulation studies and an empirical illustration using India's Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) data for 2022-23 demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed test.

items.summary: This post was written as part of the Iliad Fellowship, where I am mentored by Dmitry Vaintrob and collaborate with Brianna Grado-White. The initial inspiration came from conversation with Richard Ngo and Adrià Garriga-Alonso. To all of these my thanks. items.summary: Hyperspectral models of fish freshness rarely transfer between species, and labelling a new species is slow and destructive. Freshness is also ordinal, and standard domain alignment can erase that order. We present InvarOrd, which adapts to a new species from 30 labelled cubes (5 per rank) in three stages: self-supervised spectral pretraining on unlabelled source cubes, cross-species alignment by a shrinkage covariance discrepancy computed only within matched ranks, and ordinal distillation into a compact student. The alignment term is provably invariant to the rank means, so it gives no incentive to collapse the ordinal axis. items.summary: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.

items.summary: Safety benchmarks are cited as the primary tool to understand the risks posed by generative AI (GenAI) systems, yet growing evidence suggests they often fail to meet the needs of real-world safety evaluation. We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems. Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but…

items.summary: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. items.summary: This paper proposes a lightweight, interpretable audio anti-spoofing method that distinguishes between bona fide human speech and replay attacks by analyzing physical acoustic signatures rather than learned spectro-temporal patterns. Unlike black-box Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), our approach exploits fundamental physical invariants, specifically source kinematics, binaural phase dynamics, and aerodynamic consistency, captured via multi-channel microphone arrays. By extracting these explicit physical descriptors and classifying them with an efficient XGBoost model, we achieve detection performance (Equal Error Rate (EER) of 17.8% on 6-channel arrays) comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning baselines, but with a fraction of the computational cost. The proposed system operates with a 1 MB memory footprint and 0.9 s latency on a…

items.summary: Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be a log-concave random vector, and let $N$ be a seminorm on $\mathbb{R}^d$. For $p\ge 1$, we show that $\|N(X)\|_p$ is at most $\mathbb{E} N(X)+C s_p$, where $s_p$ is the supremum of $\|u(X)\|_p$ over all linear functionals $u$ satisfying $|u(x)|\le N(x)$ for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$. A choice for $C$ is $2+5e/2$. This bound implies Latała's conjecture on weak and strong moments.

items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs…

items.summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. items.summary: Subliminal learning is the phenomenon where a language model can learn a behavior from semantically unrelated training data. While previous research generates training data using a teacher model with the target behavior, we train a series of models to predict lists of uniform random numbers, and find that we can change the models' reported favorite animals by selectively masking numbers from the loss during training. This works best on models that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens. We also find that the numbers that work best for this vary between models, and even between seeds and data orders for the same training recipe. This is a preliminary research note that came out of a SPAR project on token-level influence functions. We expect these results to hold up, but haven't explored all possibilities and we're unsure why this…

items.summary: Medical vision--language models align radiographs with free-text reports, but radiology language distinguishes explicit findings, negation, uncertainty, and omission. Treating these report states as interchangeable during feature adaptation can change image predictions without supporting visual evidence. We introduce CARET, a parameter-efficient image-side adaptation method that retains pretrained image and text encoders and uses paired positive and negative clinical statements to define a low-dimensional semantic correction space. A bounded residual adjusts image features along these directions, while assertion-aware supervision distinguishes explicitly present and absent findings from uncertain or unmentioned ones. At inference, the adapter requires only an image; textual references remain fixed. In zero-shot classification, CARET…

items.summary: The electrocardiogram (ECG) records cardiac electrical activity across multiple leads and is used for detecting cardiac abnormalities. Recent ECG-language models enable large language models (LLMs) to interpret cardiac signals and answer clinically relevant questions. However, existing ECG-language models typically encode the ECG independently of the clinical question, forcing the ECG representation to retain broad and potentially irrelevant signal information. Moreover, these models often aggregate information across leads which can obscure lead-specific details needed for a particular question. To tackle these limitations, we introduce LEAP-LLM, an ECG-LLM architecture for Lead-aware ECG Alignment with Prompt conditioning. LEAP-LLM uses the clinical question to guide ECG feature extraction while preserving explicit lead and temporal…
items.title: LEAP-LLM: Preserving lead-time structure for question-conditioned ECG interpretation

items.summary: Efficient and secure beam alignment is essential for mmWave communication systems. However, existing deep learning (DL)-based beam alignment methods often neglect causal relationships between inputs and outputs, resulting in limited interpretability, poor generalization, and excessive beam sweeping. Moreover, these DL solutions are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small perturbations in received power measurements can mislead beam classifiers. To overcome these issues, we propose a causally-aware DL framework integrating causal discovery into beam alignment. A two-stage causal beam selection algorithm learns a Bayesian graph capturing dependencies between received signal strength indicators (RSSI) as inputs and the optimal beam index as the target variable, then uses it to select a minimal set of relevant input features for the…
items.title: Causal AI-Driven Secure mmWave Beam Alignment with Defensive Variational Autoencoders

items.summary: A runtime signature, captured without weights or response text, achieves 99.3% pair separation across 53 models. Under baseline identification and verification testing, a Claim Check against all other registered models had an AUC of 0.9997 and equal error rate of 0.5%, while held-out sessions matched their own model's signature 94.4% of the time (202 of 214), with the correct model in the top three presented every time. items.summary: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, hand-craft, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. items.summary: We propose a bound preserving finite-volume scheme for a coupled system of partial differential equations with nonlinear, nonlocal drift. The main contribution of this work is twofold: $(1)$ we show that the proposed scheme preserves physically motivated bounds; $(2)$ we prove that the scheme is well-posed and leads to a sequence of approximate solutions converging to the weak solution of the original problem. This setting is motivated by questions related to morphology formation in organic solar cells.

items.summary: Yesterday, I told my advisors that I would be dropping out of my PhD program at the University of Michigan's School of Information. I was nervous about how to break the news to them. There was already some tension in our weekly meetings: I often voiced my dissatisfaction with the pace of academia, my interests had been drifting away from theirs, and, most of all, we disagreed on the severity of the risks AI posed. When I walked into the room, they told me something I would have loved to hear months earlier: “We think it’s time to get you started on some research.” All I could say was, “I think it’s a little too late for that.” For months, I had been proposing projects that bridged my interests with theirs, such as running studies that treated humans and LLMs as equal subjects, but they were usually turned down for not being “exciting…

items.summary: Inspired by https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/xPrL2xF9iYWpPmu6B/my-empathy-is-rarely-kind I find myself confused about empathy. I wrote this to try and deconfuse myself. Let's take the example case of "posting bad political takes on the internet." When I see someone doing this, it bothers me. But then I remind myself of times that I've posted stuff that I later thought was bad. This establishes a certain baseline of empathy. But then I hit a problem: when I think back on those times, I feel shame. So though I get it, it basically justifies me feeling negative things towards them. If I feel negative towards myself for those things, it seems fair for me to send that their way. But this isn't really fair, right? I'm judging them by my own values, not theirs. There are things I've said online that I do stand behind. Presumably they feel that…
